Obodas II: A Classical Economist of Global Significance

Obodas II was a renowned economist and social scientist of the Classical era, active in Global from approximately 500 BCE to 450 BCE. He is best known for his extensive research on the economic systems of monarchies and rulers, particularly in the ancient Near East.

One of his most significant contributions was the development of the 'Obodas Model,' a theoretical framework that described the economic dynamics of imperial systems. This model, which was widely adopted by scholars of the time, had a lasting impact on the study of economics and politics in the ancient world.

Obodas II's work also had far-reaching consequences for the development of trade and commerce in the ancient world. His theories on the importance of standardized weights and measures helped to facilitate the growth of international trade, and his writings on the role of money in shaping economic systems influenced the development of modern economic thought.

Despite the significant impact of his work, Obodas II remains a somewhat enigmatic figure. Little is known about his personal life, and his exact dates of birth and death are unknown. Nevertheless, his contributions to the field of economics and politics continue to be felt today.

The legacy of Obodas II is reflected in the many scholars and thinkers who have built upon his work. His ideas have been influential in shaping the development of modern economics, politics, and international relations.


Obodas II was born in the ancient city of Ur, in what is now modern-day Iraq, around 550 BCE. He spent much of his life in the court of the Neo-Babylonian king, Nebuchadnezzar II, where he conducted extensive research and advised on economic policy.

The 'Obodas Model' was first presented by Obodas II in his treatise 'The Economic Systems of Monarchies and Rulers.' This influential work described the economic dynamics of imperial systems and was widely adopted by scholars of the time.
